listeningScripts.title: Restaurant Reservation Issue
listeningScripts.text: Diner: Hi, I made a reservation for tonight at 7 PM under the name Anderson, and I just realized the name is spelled wrong in your system. Manager: Oh no, I'm sorry about that. Let me look that up. How is it spelled? Diner: A-N-D-E-R-S-O-N. I don't know how it got misspelled. Manager: I see it here as A-N-D-E-R-S-E-N. That's an easy mix-up. When you arrive, just let the host know and we'll get you seated right away. Diner: Actually, I'm calling because I need to change the time. Can I do 7:30 instead? Manager: Absolutely. Let me adjust that for you. How many people? Diner: Six of us. Manager: Perfect. I've moved you from 7 PM to 7:30 PM for six people, and I've corrected the name spelling. Is there anything else? Diner: Yes, one more thing. Can you make sure we have a quiet table? There are some business matters we want to discuss. Manager: I'll add a note to your reservation requesting a quieter area away from the bar. We have some nice tables by the window. Diner: That sounds great. What's your cancellation policy? Manager: We require 24 hours notice for cancellations. If you need to cancel, just call us before 7:30 PM tomorrow. Diner: Got it. Thank you.

listeningScripts.title: Roommate Household Discussion
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Hey, we need to talk about the dishes piling up in the sink. Jamie: Yeah, I know. I've been really busy with work this week. Alex: I get that, but it's been sitting there for three days. Jamie: I'm sorry, I'll do them tonight. Alex: Thanks. Also, we need to talk about the grocery situation. Jamie: What do you mean? Alex: I've been buying most of the groceries, and we're not splitting the cost fairly. Jamie: You're right. How do you want to handle it? Alex: We could split everything equally, or we could each buy our own stuff separately. Jamie: I think splitting equally makes more sense. We can keep a shared list. Alex: Great. One more thing—the internet bill is due next week. It's $75 this month. Jamie: That's higher than last month. Alex: Yeah, they increased the plan by five dollars. Jamie: Okay, so $37.50 each? Alex: Exactly. I'll send you a reminder.

listeningScripts.title: Hospital Visitor Guidelines
listeningScripts.text: Welcome to City Hospital. We're glad you're visiting someone here. Please review our visitor guidelines for patient safety and comfort. Visiting hours are 10 AM to 8 PM daily. Each patient can have a maximum of two visitors at a time in their room. This ensures proper rest and medical care. Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult. We restrict visits from children with colds or contagious illnesses. Visitors should wash their hands upon arrival and before leaving. Hand-sanitizer stations are located throughout the facility. Quiet voices are required in patient rooms and hallways. Please avoid using cell phones in patient areas. Photography is not permitted without the patient's written consent. Flowers and plants are welcome, but balloons are not allowed due to interference with medical equipment. Food brought from outside is permitted only if approved by nursing staff. Many patients have dietary restrictions. Visiting a patient receiving isolation care requires special precautions. Nursing staff will provide instructions. Do not disturb patients' medical equipment, monitors, or IV lines. Visitors with concerns should speak to staff at the nursing station. Parking is available in the north lot at five dollars per visit. An elevator is located near the main entrance for easy access.

listeningScripts.title: Quebec Education Reform Approved
listeningScripts.text: The Quebec National Assembly has approved a major education reform bill with broad cross-party support. The legislation, Bill 247, focuses on modernizing curriculum standards and addressing teacher shortages. Under the new framework, high schools will introduce mandatory digital literacy courses starting next September. The reform also increases teacher salaries by 8 percent over four years to attract and retain educators. Currently, Quebec faces a shortage of approximately 3,500 teachers, particularly in mathematics, sciences, and French language instruction. The bill allocates 2.1 billion dollars for infrastructure improvements to school facilities. Education Minister Jean-François Roberge noted that 87 percent of school boards support the reforms. Parents will have increased choice in selecting specialized program options for their children. Pilot projects will begin in 15 schools across the province to test innovative teaching methods before full implementation in 2027.

listeningScripts.title: Local Food System Development
listeningScripts.text:
Farmer Cooperative Director Maria: We're launching an initiative to build a more resilient local food system for our region. Currently, about 87 percent of our food is imported from outside the province. We want to increase local food production and support our farmers. We're proposing a farmers market expansion and direct-to-consumer delivery programs. The cooperative will help coordinate logistics and marketing.

Grocery Store Manager Paul: I understand the value of local food, Maria, but I'm concerned about pricing and consistency. Local producers can't always compete with the prices we get from large distributors. And seasonality is an issue—in winter, local farmers have limited options. My customers expect year-round availability and competitive pricing.

Public Health Officer Dr. Sarah: Actually, Paul, local food systems have documented health benefits. Communities with stronger local food networks show 22 percent higher rates of fresh produce consumption. Plus, reducing transportation distance improves food safety and nutrition because products reach consumers fresher. And we should consider the long-term economic impact. Local spending circulates within the community.

Small Farm Owner James: I'd love to participate in this initiative. Currently, I sell about 40 percent of my production to the farmers market, but I'd like to do more direct sales. The issue is I don't have the infrastructure for packaging and distribution. If the cooperative could help with that, I could increase production by 60 percent.

listeningScripts.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
listeningScripts.text: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.
